## ARGUMENT

### I. An Employer That Abandons the Interactive Process Is Liable Under the ADA When Its Failure Keeps a Reasonable Accommodation from Being Identified.

The ADA defines discrimination to include failing to make "reasonable accommodations to the known physical or mental limitations" of a qualified individual. 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5)(A). The implementing regulation contemplates an "informal, interactive process" to identify the limitation and the accommodations that might overcome it. 29 C.F.R. § 1630.2(o)(3). This Court has long treated that process as the means by which the statutory duty is carried out. *Beck v. Univ. of Wis. Bd. of Regents*, 75 F.3d 1130, 1135–36 (7th Cir. 1996); *Bultemeyer v. Fort Wayne Cmty. Schs.*, 100 F.3d 1281, 1285 (7th Cir. 1996).

**A. The duty is shared, but the employer cannot excuse its own breakdown.**

Both parties must participate in good faith. When the process fails, the question is who caused the failure. *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135–37. An employer that is responsible for the breakdown cannot defend on the ground that the employee failed to propose the right accommodation. *Bultemeyer* rejected that argument where the employee had put the employer on notice of his limitations and the employer did not seek clarification or explore alternatives. 100 F.3d at 1285–86. The employee need not use particular words or present a fully formed proposal. Once the employer knows of the disability and the need for accommodation, the duty to engage is triggered. *Id.*; *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135.

**B. Liability attaches when the employer's failure prevents identification of an accommodation.**

The Court has been precise about when a failure to engage becomes actionable. The failure is not a freestanding violation. It is actionable when it keeps the parties from finding an accommodation that would have enabled the employee to perform the essential functions of the job. *Rehling v. City of Chicago*, 207 F.3d 1009, 1015–16 (7th Cir. 2000); *Jackson v. City of Chicago*, 414 F.3d 806, 813 (7th Cir. 2005); *EEOC v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 417 F.3d 789, 805–07 (7th Cir. 2005). That rule reflects the practical problem the process exists to solve. An employee often cannot know which accommodations are feasible in a particular workplace, because the employer holds the information about job structure, alternative positions, equipment, and scheduling. An employer that refuses to engage withholds that information and then points to the employee's failure to identify a solution. This Court has not allowed employers to do that. *See Sears*, 417 F.3d at 805–08 (reversing where the employer's own conduct undermined the process).

Accordingly, the employee's burden is to show that a reasonable accommodation was possible. The employee need not show that the employee would have identified it unaided. *See Jackson*, 414 F.3d at 813; *Sears*, 417 F.3d at 806–07. Where the record permits a reasonable inference that good-faith engagement would have produced a workable accommodation, summary judgment for the employer is improper. *Spurling v. C & M Fine Pack, Inc.*, 739 F.3d 1055, 1061–62 (7th Cir. 2014).

**C. Plaintiff's showing satisfies this standard.**

*Basden v. Professional Transportation, Inc.*, 714 F.3d 1034, 1037–39 (7th Cir. 2013), confirms the limits of the rule. A plaintiff who cannot show that any accommodation would have allowed him to perform the job cannot rely on process failures alone. This case is different. Plaintiff notified Defendant of the limitation and requested accommodation. Defendant did not seek clarifying medical information, discuss alternatives, or explain why the request could not be met. [Record cites.] Plaintiff has identified specific accommodations that were available and would have enabled performance of the essential job functions. [Record cites.] Defendant, not Plaintiff, was responsible for the breakdown. *Beck*, 75 F.3d at 1135–37; *Bultemeyer*, 100 F.3d at 1285–86. Because that breakdown prevented the parties from settling on an accommodation that a reasonable factfinder could find feasible, Defendant is liable under § 12112(b)(5)(A). *Rehling*, 207 F.3d at 1015–16.
